title: Classes, objects and encapsulation
description: Classes and objects, access modifiers, properties, constructors and static members.

content.title: Classes and objects

choices.text: 1 class, 2 objects
2 classes, 2 objects
2 classes, 1 object
1 class, 1 object

content.explanation: Dog is one class (the blueprint). Each new creates a separate object (an instance), so there are two dogs.

content.question: What is a constructor for?

choices.text: Putting a new object in a valid state when it is created
Destroying the object when it is no longer used
Copying an object into another one
Declaring which methods a class must have

content.explanation: A constructor runs once, when new creates the object. Requiring the needed values there (like the dog's name) means no object can exist half-built.

content.title: Encapsulation
content.body:
Encapsulation means an object hides its internal state and only lets others use it through its methods and properties. The object stays in charge of its own rules.

Access modifiers decide who can use a member:
- public: everyone.
- private: only the class itself (the default for members).
- protected: the class and the classes that inherit from it.
- internal: any code in the same assembly (project).

A property like public decimal Balance { get; private set; } can be read by everyone, but only changed by the class.

choices.text: So that the balance can only change through Deposit, which checks the amount
To make reading the balance faster
Because properties of type decimal must have a private setter
So that the balance cannot be read outside the class

content.explanation: That is encapsulation: other code can read Balance, but cannot write Balance = -1000 and skip the rules. Reading is still public thanks to the public get.

content.question: A method is declared without any access modifier: void Recalculate() { ... } inside a class. Who can call it?

choices.text: Only the class itself: members are private by default
Everyone: members are public by default
The classes of the same project
The classes that inherit from it

content.explanation: In a class, members without a modifier are private. Being explicit is still a good habit, so readers do not have to remember the rule.

content.question: Which modifier lets any code in the same project use a member, but no code in other projects?

choices.text: internal
protected
private
public

content.explanation: internal means "visible inside this assembly". It is handy for helpers that other projects should not depend on.

choices.text: Total is 2 and a.Mine is 1
Total is 1 and a.Mine is 1
Total is 2 and a.Mine is 2
Total is 1 and a.Mine is 2

content.explanation: A static field belongs to the class and is shared by all objects: both clicks add to the same Total. Mine is an instance field: each counter has its own.

content.question: Which are good encapsulation habits?

choices.text: Keep fields private and expose properties or methods
Check the rules in the methods that change the object, so it always stays valid
Make every field public, it is simpler
Return your internal List<T> directly so callers can add items to it

content.explanation: Returning the internal list lets anyone change it without going through your rules. Return a read-only view (IReadOnlyList<T>) or a copy instead.

content.instructions: Match each keyword with what it means.

pairs.definition: Usable by the class and the classes that inherit from it
Usable by any code in the same assembly
Belongs to the class itself, shared by all its objects
A field that can only be set in its declaration or in a constructor
